newsitem.title: UK: Target dates set for SIB proposals on LME - King.
newsitem.headline: Target dates set for SIB proposals on LME - King.

text.p: The London Metal Exchange (LME) has set target dates for market reform following the 1996 Sumitomo copper scandal, LME Chief Executive David King said on Thursday.
Reform proposals by Britain's Securities and Investments Board (SIB) cover changes to price transparency, governance of the Exchange and warehousing.
King said various proposals were made to the LME's Board at its Wednesday meeting and approved.
"We indicated a target date for completion of each of these recommendations," he said.
The timeframe for implementing the SIB proposals depends on the issue being addressed, and dates vary between January 1997, through 1997 to the year-end.
In most cases, SIB's proposals can be implemented speedily, although some may require three months' notice, which is standard practice regarding LME contracts, he said.
King identified three areas covered by the SIB review that the LME will be addressing in coming months.
Firstly, governance of the LME will require changes to the market's articles of association and this will need to be presented to members at an Extraordinary General Meeting (EGM).
Secondly, rule changes will need consideration by the LME's committees, and may need consultations with members and Board approval, he said.
Finally, technological issues will need evaluating on a cost-benefit basis and then tenders will have to be put out for the work to be carried out.

One element covered by this is SIB's proposal that the LME study the introduction of electronic paperless transfer of warrants. Warrants are the bearer documents of title to metal stored in LME-registered warehouses.
The LME previously looked at what it called a Warrant Automated Depository System (WADS), but did not proceed because the costs outweighed the benefits at that time, King said.

However, the LME has already carried out some work with the London Clearing House (LCH) regarding WADS. But the timetable for introducing WADS has to fit in not only with the LME and the LCH, but warehouses and market-members, he said.
"The only possible over-run (on SIB's proposals) would be the WADS project," King said.

The LME Board has also authorised an increase in charges to members to cover the costs involved in adopting the SIB measures, as well as a 20 percent expansion in the LME Secretariat's personnel, King added.
The SIB, Britain's top regulator, was asked by the LME to carry out a wide-ranging review of the market after the Sumitomo Corp scandal shocked world markets in June 1996.
In mid-June, Sumitomo fired its head copper trader Yasuo Hamanaka, alleging he had admitted running up losses of $2.6 billion in unauthorised copper trading.
The SIB issued its report and recommendations in December, with the LME making its formal response after Wednesday's monthly Board meeting.
